events.title: Banks rescue a large investment fund
events.description: Private banks and securities firms invest in Long-Term Capital Management after heavy losses.

events.title: The euro begins
events.description: Eleven countries adopt a shared currency for financial transactions. Notes and coins come later.

events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands in the United States. Communities mourn and help those affected.

what_happened_next.text:
Bonds led this group over five years. The U.S. share basket finished only a little higher, while the international basket and all three featured companies ended lower: Disney near 68 cents per starting dollar, Nike near 81 cents and Intel near 83 cents. This was a hard window for stock investors, but it does not prove that stocks always lose or bonds always win.

Each company faced a different business story. Disney’s California Adventure opened in 2001 and helped lift resort visits, but the added costs weighed on Parks & Resorts operating income. Nike’s 1998 income fell nearly half amid softer demand and excess inventory. Intel reported that 2001 revenue dropped 21% as computer demand weakened. One company’s challenge did not make the others’ results identical.

The years also included the rescue of Long-Term Capital Management, the euro’s start for financial transactions and the September 11 attacks. The bond choice did well in this window while the three company shares fell. That comparison shows how spreading money among different kinds of investments can change the result, but bonds can also lose value in other periods.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Thailand changed its currency policy, index funds were drawing money, and companies were changing leaders and products.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The investment mix mattered. Cash and the government-bond choice rose while many shares fell. They did not depend on a particular company succeeding.
reflection.what_faded_away: A well-known brand and a popular theater production did not prevent losses in a company’s shares. Recent market success was not a promise of five more good years.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: The coming sequence of crises and market falls was unknown. A sensible plan still had to allow for outcomes that the starting headlines did not predict.

hot:1997-07:disney.text: Disney California Adventure and two nearby resort additions opened on February 8, 2001. The attractions and hotels brought more visitors and guest spending, but Parks & Resorts operating income fell 2% in fiscal 2001 as costs also rose.

hot:1997-07:nike.text: Nike’s fiscal 1998 revenue rose 4% to a record $9.6 billion, but net income fell nearly half to $399.6 million. Weak demand and extra inventory led to discounting, squeezing profit even as sales reached a record.

hot:1997-07:intel.text: Intel reported 2001 revenue of $26.5 billion in January 2002, down 21% from 2000, and its net income also dropped sharply. Weaker computer demand after the technology boom meant fewer chip orders, leaving Intel with a difficult sales year.
